speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The brokenness of drugs is more than statistics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have felt that brokenness on the ground.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before entering politics, I volunteered at the Singapore Anti-Narcotics Association to work with youths-at-risk and speak about the havoc drugs can create in their young lives.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Drug addiction, for many, is the death of their drive and ambition.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) and the Singapore Prison Service are sterling institutions, staffed with dedicated and committed officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Their effort in the fight against drugs is courageous.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, the fight is not only theirs to bear.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first point is that we need to deter drug trafficking in Singapore and into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Stemming the supply of drugs is a critical part of the fight against drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We want a drug-free Singapore, not a drug-tolerant Singapore." These positions, which support a tough stance on drugs, should remain.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The next year, 2015, the demand for cannabis increased.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One year later, in 2016, the amount of cannabis seized continued to rise significantly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: According to provisional statistics, during the first six months of 2016, the amount of cannabis seized was almost the same amount for the entire year of 2015.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Therefore, muscular laws continue to be needed as they are both relevant and necessary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Stopping drugs from entering Singapore is an important aspect of solving the drug problem.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To stem the supply of drugs, we need tough laws to deter the potential drug trafficker.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: After all, drug trafficking is, for the most part, pre-meditated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is a coldly calculated risk between potential profit and potential punishment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What does one stand to gain from drug trafficking?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Driven by greed, the drug trafficker takes the plunge.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He lines his pocket with money at the expense of the drug addict, the addict's family and society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These tough laws are needed to deter harm − to deter harm to the abuser and to society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We must hold the line of tough and muscular laws.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We must strengthen this line, defend it and protect it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When a person becomes a drug addict, nothing else matters.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He neglects his children, his parents, his job and his own health.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For example, the severe condition of "meth mouth" is associated with drug use − multiple teeth decay, teeth breaking completely at the gum line, gum disease and bone loss.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Even in low doses, permanent brain damage may result: using cannabis as rare as once a week may irreversibly lower one's IQ.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I completely disagree with the term "soft" drug.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There is nothing soft about the ill-effects of drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Multiple studies have shown that cannabis can be a gateway drug to heroin and cocaine, especially among young abusers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Compared to the general population, there is a four-fold higher risk of mortality among those with cannabis-use disorder.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To escape the clutches of illicit drug taking, some addicts have to endure excruciating symptoms, such as uncontrollable vomiting and diarrhoea and an unstoppable feeling of insects crawling under his skin.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: After overcoming addiction, the ex-addict would still need to battle the lure of drugs that will come back to haunt him throughout his life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is not only the drug addict who is harmed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: His family and those around him are deeply affected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A drug addict's ability to communicate and maintain good relationships is impaired.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: His mother, father, husband, wife, son, daughter, employee or employer will be affected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The physically and emotionally absent addict puts a strain on the family unit he is in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Last year, a picture from Ohio made its round around the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It showed a four-year-old child left in a car with two adults overdosing and unconscious.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A month later, yet another harrowing picture − this time, a 10-month-old infant in the backseat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To drive the point further on the harmfulness of drugs, let us do some sums.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How many people does one think are affected by a drug trafficker who has trafficked the amount of drugs which may attract the death penalty?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If one multiplies those numbers with the number of family members affected, the impact of drug trafficking is severely expanded.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Let us say, for each addict, he has a spouse, a parent and two children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That means five people are affected − the addict himself and four family members.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Multiplying 180 abusers a week by five, we get about 900 people affected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If a person ran towards 30 platoons with a grenade, should not a lethal shot be fired to protect the 900 people?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We need tough drug laws to prevent the immense harm drug trafficking inflicts on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These families are psychologically crippled over weeks, months, years; slowly, insidiously.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Not only are the drug addict and his family affected by the actions of the drug trafficker, society is affected as well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Drug addicts need increasing doses of drugs to feel normal or to feel the next high.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As a result, many resort to crime to fund their addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With an increase in crime rate, the security and peaceful environment we enjoy and take for granted will become threatened.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is for these reasons that I seek that the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) be reviewed regularly so as to ensure that it contains the legal muscle it needs to deter the supply, that is, trafficking, and the demand, being the consumption − both elements of the drug offence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I call for a regular overview of the MDA.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In 2014, the percentage of young abusers under the age of 30, compared to overall abusers, was 35.1%.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Furthermore, in 2015 and 2016, the number of new drug abusers increased.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Among the new drug abusers, close to two-thirds are below 30 years of age.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The second reason why I ask for a review of the MDA is that the supply of cannabis is on an upward trend.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In fact, the provisional statistics for January to June 2016 showed that the amount of cannabis seized in that six-month period was almost the same amount for the entire year of 2015.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Another statistic of concern is the number of penal drug admissions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In 2011, the number of penal drug admissions decreased to an all-time low of 1,742.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The reply to a Parliamentary Question in September last year seems to suggest that trafficking has increased from 2011 and that the present figures remain higher than in 2011.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For several years, in the constituency I serve, we helped a grandmother raise her grandson.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Her daughter got hooked on drugs and spent time in prison.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: On top of her work as a cleaner, this devoted grandmother saw to her grandson's needs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When he did well in school, we all celebrated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But there is a missing link − his mother.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When his mother was going to be released from the DRC, I wrote a letter to her personally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We wanted her to know what her own mother had to go through because of her drug addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We wanted her not to return to her old ways.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In that letter, we offered her a job − a job that was near her house.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We wanted her to be able to support her family and be there for her son.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the end, she thanked us but found somewhere else to work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Just five days ago, at my MPS on Friday night, I met an aged grandmother.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Because her son and her daughter-in-law are in prison.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The grandmother needs to take care of her grandchild's schooling, sustenance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Drug traffickers destroy lives and such destruction can be inter-generational.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I ask this House, do we let the supply of drugs overtake us?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is suggested that we revisit the law regularly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Through such regular reviews, the benefits and possible gaps in existing laws should become more evident.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One aspect to re-examine under a review is whether the law, as presently encapsulated in the MDA, can be better calibrated to address the harmfulness of newer drugs or drug combinations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For example, drugs are often mixed with contaminants or with other illicit drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These contaminants may affect the potency and addictiveness of the drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One recent example in America was heroin mixed with elephant tranquiliser.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This potent mixture caused many to overdose and die.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This contamination is driven by greed − more effect, with lower cost to produce.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The meat tenderiser, which is normally used to "pre-digest" meat to make it tender, is mixed with the drug such that it "dissolves muscle and flesh" when administered.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Essentially, we need to look at the detrimental effects of drugs in the raw, in the flesh and without rose-tinted glasses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is named after the side-effects, crocodile-like skin − green, scaly and bumpy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If it misses the vein, it eats the flesh.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It has been described as destroying "body tissue the way battery acid eats through plastic".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Yet, this harmful drug made of codeine mixed with lighter fluid, industrial cleaning oil or the like, is three times cheaper to produce than heroin.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This brings into sharp focus why we need to do all we can to ensure that drugs do not get a foothold, in particular.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Hence, the MDA should not only be focused on the weight of the drugs trafficked but should also give due consideration to the potential harmfulness of the drug when mixed or cocktailed with available consumables.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The second suggestion is that we would need quicker incorporation of new drugs into the First Schedule.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The "First Schedule" should be "flexible" enough to quickly incorporate new drugs not previously outlawed, especially since new concoctions are constantly being attempted at by syndicates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This slide illustrates that it is important that our laws be able to keep up with New Psychoactive Substances (NPS).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What is currently done by the Fifth Schedule which allows for "restricted circulation" is a good measure, but it is imperative for effective control of addiction that the move to make such substances "First Schedule" be prompt, that is, be prompt enough to frame a drug trafficking charge against it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The third suggestion is to insert a new provision in the MDA, creating a unique offence of sale of drugs over the Internet, attracting a higher penalty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Most commonly described as the Dark Net, more people are turning to the Internet to get their next fix.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean also mentioned at the 5th ASEAN Ministerial Meeting on Drugs that "illicit dealers… used the Dark Net to attract new drug abusers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Due to the increasing number of youths experimenting with drugs and the huge potential of the Internet to facilitate sales to youth, we should consider specifically how an aggravated offence can be legislated where the trafficker uses any element of social media or the Internet to entice or procure sales.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This may deter drug traffickers from using the Internet to advertise sales, potentially leading to reduced drug sales to youth.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In particular, messaging applications, such as WhatsApp, often used by the younger generation, should be covered.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Now, I move on to the second point which is why we need to invest in rehabilitation so as to reduce the recidivism rate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Helping those who have fallen into drug addiction to get out of it is just as important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There are several reasons why rehabilitation is important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Drug trafficking laws need to be tough − deterrence is the main reason for punishment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is only right for a premeditated, greed-driven crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They need to get out of the clutches of drug addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Yes, it is right that we have the Drug Rehabilitation Centre to rehabilitate our drug addicts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Let us remember − it is the Drug Rehabilitation Centre.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We have already chosen to subscribe to the philosophy of rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For those six months to three years, we have chosen to take custody of the drug addict in order to rehabilitate him.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is only proper that we give the drug addict the best shot at turning over a new leaf.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Each addict saved means another husband, wife or child saved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Each addict saved means one more valuable contributor to our society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Each addict saved is a life saved − a life saved from misery, self-harm, lost potential.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In order to rehabilitate well, we need to look surgically at our recidivism rate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These are all good initiatives and recommendations, but there is a lot more we can do.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Rehabilitation is, by its very nature, always a work in progress and I acknowledge the good work the Prison Service does in this regard.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I also accept that there must also be a strong desire on the part of the drug addict to want to rehabilitate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I hope the following suggestions could be taken into consideration, with the mind of developing and adding to the Prison's good work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The first suggestion is to increase access to effective rehabilitation for lower risk inmates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We should make full use of the window of opportunity while an addict is low-risk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Lower risk inmates have a higher chance of recovery.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If that opportunity is not grasped and he did not have the best chance for rehabilitation, he will soon relapse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is even more important for young drug abusers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Youthful years are meant to develop a good circle of friends and good peer support.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That is why investing in the rehabilitation of young drug abusers is so important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But how can we do this effectively for the young drug abuser, as well as the older drug abuser?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A key method of reconditioning is pleasure replacement.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When drugs are used to escape from difficult situations, it is important for rehabilitation that ex-drug addicts experience that there are other healthier ways of getting relief.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For instance, physical activity and games help re-write the circuit and show that, yes, there can be relief outside drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Such activities also foster motivation through goal-setting and working towards a drug-free life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The idea is pleasure replacement − replacing the pleasure derived from drugs with more healthy activities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We should study to see how such models can be transferred into a DRC setting.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With that, let me move on to reintegration, which is another key factor in lowering recidivism, which is a key component for rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the DRC, counselling on resisting the temptation to take drugs is head knowledge.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But once the addict is released, he is plunged into a world where the temptations lurk about.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The ex-drug addict needs to have counsellors available to him, post-release, to help him.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One such support mechanism is the Serigaya Methamphetamine Relapse Prevention Program (SMARPP), a work-book based counselling exercise, in Japan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would the good Minister consider issuing a self-teaching workbook to each ex-drug addict upon release as a resource to help him resist the urge to do drugs?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Family, Madam, plays an important role in the reintegration of an ex-drug addict.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Families need to be equipped and empowered to fulfil their roles as the anchors they can be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A proactive family may ask these questions: how best to help the ex-offender?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Families need to be equipped with the answers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There may be shock, denial, hurt, a sense of betrayal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But, ultimately, who would not want their husband, father, son, or wife, mother or daughter back?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The suggestion here is that DRC inmates be given more visitation time to facilitate the reintegration process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Family therapy is an initiative that could be looked into seriously within the DRC, attended by the inmates and their families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Another idea is for more families to attend family-focused workshops, like those conducted in 2006 by the Family Resource Centre.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Topics were based on inmates' needs, as identified by their personal supervisors in prison, including parental, marital and reintegration issues.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The suggestion here is to have a larger number of joint sessions involving the inmate and his family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For those with little or no family support, positive peer support can come in the way of Community Befrienders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The volunteer's role is important, especially since a new social network is critical for disengaging from the web of drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While muscular laws and effective rehabilitation are needed to combat the supply and demand elements of drug offences, we must also ensure that the overall national attitude or the cultural perception towards drugs remains strongly anti-drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We, as a society, must view drug trafficking and consumption with suspicion and disapproval.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We cannot afford to slip into a pro-drug culture.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Many countries have lost the war on drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In a defeatist narrative, these countries now proclaim the usefulness of "soft" drugs, such as cannabis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Such a narrative paints these soft drugs as harmless.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Such spiel may sound attractive, but what it really indicates is that those countries are on the back foot in their already-weak fight against drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That narrative, though false, has permeated through the globe, such that a culture more tolerant to recreational drug use is setting root.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Singapore could fall prey to such a culture.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We should reveal drugs for what they really are − harmful, addictive, destructive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The drug endemic in America is a prime example of what we should not allow to happen on our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There, drugs are not just tolerated but also promoted.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Lives are wasted, potential is wasted − all because of higher tolerance, which blossoms into the acceptance of a drug culture.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Please look, in particular, at the line that extends all the way to 2015 − the percentage of traffic accidents in Washington where drivers have been tested positive for the active ingredient in cannabis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That has steadily increased since 2012 and has climbed rapidly upward.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The prevalence of drug abuse has also impacted the economy of Colorado.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Large businesses now have to recruit out-of-state residents to find employees that can pass a pre-employment drug test.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As a pre-construction company told The New York Times, "to find a roofer or a painter that can pass a drug test is unheard of." This slide shows an increase in calls, relating to cannabis, to the Poison Centre in Washington state.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This means that even with restrictions on buying cannabis, more people unintentionally ingest cannabis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is true even among those under 20.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Most of the time, the cannabis came from family or friends.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Attractive edible cannabis caused half of the known exposures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The pictures on this slide show edible cannabis and they give you an idea of how children can be so easily attracted to it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Do we want to expose our children to this on our shores?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We need to expose these pro-drug lies for what they really are − out for profit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The pro-drug camp wraps lies in a palatable way, with phrases like − "right to do recreational drugs", "victimless crime", "harm reduction." The shift in drug policy around the world is not driven by truth about drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Rather, in my view, a drug-tolerant culture is fuelled by those who stand to profit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Harm reduction is a subversive slogan that calls for a permissive attitude towards drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is touted as pre-emptive, not punitive, not deterrent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But in reality, it is a mere surrender on the war on drugs − it was exceptionally difficult in those countries to substantially stem the supply of drugs into their borders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We need to start young and reinforce it regularly by putting it in the Primary and Secondary school syllabus.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Another important aspect of exposing propaganda is not just telling the truth, but also teaching how to find the truth.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is especially important as young people increasingly turn to the Internet as a source of information.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Hence, it is important that students be equipped with the skills to (a) find credible sources of information and (b) be alert to the rhetoric used by the pro-drug camp.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Pro-drug rhetoric says that drugs will solve problems, but is there another solution?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: People need to know that there is another solution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Started in Sweden, Mentor International, "provide(s) support, best practices and evidence-based mentoring programs that offer young people the inspiration, empowerment and motivation they need to make healthy life choices and view their futures more positively." The idea behind it is for students to have a guide to navigate through life − this increases the propensity to stay clear of drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Parents play a big role in drug prevention.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There are two things that people, generally, and parents, in particular, in my view, need to know even before they are ready to hear any information they need to on drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They need to know that: (a) it is a matter that they should be concerned about; and (b) that they matter − that parents matter.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Where the family is dysfunctional, a good peer group is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If no good peer group exists, then the at-risk youth needs to equip himself with ways to disbelieve that drugs are good.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I have given some examples of how the at-risk youth can equip himself.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Ultimately, the anti-drug culture must win the war against pro-drug propaganda.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The mindshare of Singapore's youth is a key battleground − the pro-drug camp must be defeated there.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The drug scourge in Singapore, while numbers are relatively low compared to many developed countries, still remains a cause for concern.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: According to our Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) 2016 report on the drug situation in Singapore, there are two trends that merit serious concerns.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2015, there were 1,309 new drug abusers arrested.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Almost two-thirds of these new abusers are below 30 years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, out of the total of 3,245 drug abusers arrested in 2016, slightly over 40% of them are below 30 years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, CNB has also seen an increase in online drug peddling last year.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a five-and-a-half time increase in numbers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such liberal attitudes towards drug use cannot be tolerated.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The harmful effects of drugs may not be fully understood by the young people who are using drugs, who may believe that recreational use of drugs is well within their control and that they will not be addicted to it, or that there will not be any damaging long-term effects on their physical or mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While CNB may have stepped up its youth outreach efforts through the use of technology and social media, a more targeted approach framework needs to be found to specifically reach out to Primary and Secondary school students and students studying in our post-Secondary institutions, starting with those who are in their early to mid-teens.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My 18-year-old son, who is studying in a local polytechnic, shares with me about two of his friends who are not just smoking cigarettes, but also taking drugs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are quite nonchalant about it and seem to think it is no big deal.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They even offered my son to smoke weed or join them in taking a puff to get high, to which he sensibly and thankfully declined.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of his friends, also a polytechnic student, smokes weed or marijuana in the polytechnic itself.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another of his friends is an ITE student who was caught for smoking weed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While he is undergoing follow-up checks through routine urine tests, he continues to take synthetic weed, which he claims cannot be detected through the urine tests.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This outreach, engagement and targeted public education against drug use and abuse should also be done concurrently with the fight against smoking.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To me, the addiction to smoking and drug use is one and the same, and should be done in tandem, since the smoking habit seems to create a propensity towards smoking or taking drugs as well.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Never mind that the amount of drugs is small, and never mind that the perpetrators are committing it for the first time, but that they are young.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We do not tolerate drug trafficking and use.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this point, Deputy Speaker, Sir, please allow me to continue in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   The war on drugs is a joint effort by all of us.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need pervasive approaches so as to reach out to and educate our young on the damaging and irreversible effects of both smoking and drug use.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Support and assistance from influential personalities and positive role models that our young look up to, strengthen this approach.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that local personalities, such as Taufik Batisah and Irfan Fandi, have joined in this fight against drug abuse by offering their time and energy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to more support from such personalities and positive role models for our young.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, support from home is also important in shaping positive mindsets among our youths in this fight against drug abuse.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need parents to be positive role models for their children − not just by advising them to stay drug-free or smoke-free − but to also role model positive behaviour and healthy lifestyles, free from addiction of any sort.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This reminds me of one of my residents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ms Lydia is still relatively young, barely 40 years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But each time I met her, she looked haggard and worried, as though she was over 50 years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Her husband is incarcerated because of drug abuse even though he is already in his 50s.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And this is not the first time he had been in prison because of drugs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have three children − two studying in primary school and one who is three years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Throughout the time Ms Lydia is married to her husband, she did not work and depended on him for financial support.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With her husband's recent incarceration, Ms Lydia finds herself with no source of income.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We tried our best to help her by providing her with temporary financial assistance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we also helped Ms Lydia find part-time work and get a place for her youngest child in a childcare centre so that Ms Lydia can work.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although Ms Lydia is a strong woman who remains undaunted, the social and emotional impact on her and her children, who are now unable to see their father, is quite deep and cannot be easily forgotten.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Support from the family is much needed, not just when our children or family member have succumbed to drug addiction or smoking, but even before they become a slave to addiction.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Developing positive habits and a healthy lifestyle − such as doing sports as a family, spending time on a common hobby with family members and close friends, or by volunteering and doing meaningful work for our community − will help each and every one of us to keep addiction at bay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): I must admit that the drug scourge in Singapore is not isolated or that only our local agencies have to step up in terms of outreach, education and enforcement.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The drug scourge is certainly a global one.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Getting rid of an addiction is certainly not easy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It takes a lot of courage, discipline and inner strength and, of course, support from our loved ones.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When it comes to addiction: "I can choose to let it define me; confine me; outshine me; or I can choose to move on and leave it behind me." Thank you, Sir.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's small size, tough laws and the dedication of the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) to their mission have made this possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reality of governments in other parts of the world is very different.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At best, this has to do with being a larger polity and the difficulty in ensuring that the writ of the state extends across hundreds and thousands of kilometres, different political cultures, different social circumstances and different norms that govern individual freedoms and liberties.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At worst, it is a self-evident reality that the world-wide war against drugs has failed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Whichever perspective one takes, these realities have precipitated a new and different approach now taken globally to deal with the drug problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A major plank of this new approach calls for the legalisation of drug use, particularly in medical marijuana on health grounds and, in some jurisdictions, the legalisation of recreational drugs per se.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2001, an Economist article titled "The Case for Legalisation" argued that a legal market for drugs would be the best guarantee that drug-taking would be no more dangerous than smoking and drinking, even as it acknowledged that legalisation would not be easy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fast forward just about 15 years and the first sentence of a piece on the legalisation of drugs in the same publication went like this: "The argument for the legalisation of cannabis has been won." In so far as global trends are concerned, the movement to legalise drugs is now effectively mainstream.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Closer to home, attitudes are shifting, too, mainly with a view to get a better handle on the drug problem and to undermine organised crime.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Senior Vice-Chairman of the Malaysian Crime Prevention Council, Tan Sri Lee Lam Thye, in a piece titled "Consider Less Severe Punishment" in the New Straits Times last year, noted that despite punitive laws against illicit drugs, capital punishment and spending millions to address the problem, the number of addicts in Malaysia was growing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He called on the Malaysian authorities to consider "the road less travelled" and to decriminalise drug use and possession and to treat drug addiction as a medical problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, late last year, the Thai Cabinet approved the proposal to allow hemp, a plant which is part of the cannabis family, but with lesser amounts of the psychoactive substance tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) to be grown as a cash crop as part of a project to use narcotic plants for medicinal purposes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prior to the Cabinet decision, Thailand's Justice Minister General Paiboon Koomchaya was quoted in the Thai media as saying that he was firm in his aim to remove marijuana from the narcotics drugs list and to treat it as a medicinal herb.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The movement towards the gradual acceptance of some drugs, chiefly cannabis, for medical purposes is a powerful catalyst in the case for the legalisation of drugs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if medical authorities have not ruled definitively in this area and medical practitioners argued that there are realistic alternatives to medical marijuana, nevertheless, an international industry has already taken form and a stronger lobby is likely to follow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the Guardian has reported research in Israel will transform the medical marijuana industry into, and I quote, "a serious endeavour of pharmaceutical research producing new strains and drugs able to alleviate the symptoms of cancer, Parkinson's disease, insomnia and other conditions." With the advances in technology, many Israeli companies are working to develop medicine that can deliver precise doses of THC so as to allegedly regulate its psychoactive effects, with the view to bring relief to those in chronic pain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is repeated around the world where fierce debates about legalisation are taking place and have taken place, is the emotionally powerful argument that medical marijuana has eased the suffering of those in pain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is also fathomable that the research into medical marijuana will have a direct bearing on the use of recreational marijuana for which precise doses could also correspondingly be marketed as a safer means of drug consumption.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is likely to accelerate the legalisation of drugs worldwide is the potential of regulation and taxation, with recreational usage potentially effectively killing off the profits earned by drug cartels and moving them into state and corporate coffers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The challenge, of course, is setting the appropriate tax rate in many jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would hazard that the attraction of taxation may prove irresistible for those governments that have not been able to successfully keep drugs out of mainstream society in the same way Singapore has been able to.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our tough laws will continue to serve as a deterrent for some drug traffickers but I am concerned we will find it increasingly difficult to persuade younger Singaporeans, particularly those who venture overseas for studies or business, about the dangers of drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The somewhat emotionally persuasive argument of medical marijuana in spite of a currently more established medical opinion will make this even harder.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, with a large population of foreigners, many of whom are transient residents, living and working in Singapore, and a significant number of overseas Singaporeans who may have a very different cultural attitude towards drugs, the argument for a drug-free Singapore may also increasingly come under strain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, we should and must begin preparing for a much tougher environment in the immediate term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not only if the research on medical marijuana turns decidedly positive for some reason.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As drug syndicates are put out of business because of legalisation, some of them, some drug traffickers or abusers, may paradoxically choose to target Singapore from the confines of other countries if there is money to be made here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those who will fall foul of our tough drug laws will not be the kingpins but the couriers, many of whom seek to make a quick buck.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We may also expect to see a rise in the number of marijuana abuses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, a Facebook page titled "Singapore cannabis awareness" has already generated close to 4,000 likes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It makes a point to track changing norms about the legalisation of cannabis around the world, recently posting a story about the state of New South Wales in Australia funding the world's first clinical trial for the use of cannabis in alleviating chemotherapy inducing vomiting and nausea.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not fake news, for such trials are indeed ongoing, but the practical effect of such developments around the world, I fear, will likely result in a more relaxed attitude towards the usage of cannabis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For those who believe that a more permissive environment for recreational consumption of drugs in Singapore would not necessarily be hazardous, I would say, be careful what you wish for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And that prospect, should there be arguments made about the drug tolerance regime in Singapore, is scary and wholly unwelcomed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As it stands, the argument for the legalisation of drugs in Singapore, in particular, is not compelling or persuasive at all.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mr Deputy Speaker, strict laws can only do so much, even if they host a deterrent effect.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my ward of Eunos in Aljunied GRC in years past, I have worked with the Central Narcotics Bureau and conducted preventive education talks at our local mosque with the permission of the mosque community and I thank them for their support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At schools and tertiary institutions, in particular, we will have to significantly step up preventive education and to prepare our children and young adults for the world of tomorrow where access to drugs will be more commonplace than ever before and in our mindshare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government would also have to focus more squarely on the permissive attitudes that are hardening in favour of supposedly softer drugs like cannabis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is harmful to one's health and not every citizen will have ready access or support from family members to rehabilitative resources.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As it is usually the case with illegal drugs, the poor and the low-income will be the hardest hit.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I remember, many years ago, as a young junior doctor, looking after a young mother, whose life had been ruined by drugs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She had been abusing her drugs, injecting herself.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Germs went to her heart, eating away one of her heart valves, so her heart could not pump properly.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The germs from the injection continued to spread, to her lungs and the rest of her body.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is what drug abuse did to her.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A young mother, young children, their future taken away.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The drugs did not give her a chance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The person who introduced her to drug abuse, he did not give her a chance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Every person who continued to sell her illegal drugs for abuse, they never gave her a chance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And we can also look to other countries like America, to see the extent of the problem.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This does not even count the rate of drug-related crime: gang violence, robbery, murder, crimes under the influence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we look at countries that have taken a soft approach, there is no straightforward way for these countries to roll back the situation because drugs have become so entrenched.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You can see it in the United States.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You can see it in parts of the West.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What we decide today shapes the course of a generation to come.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to care and we need to be careful when certain propagandists, when certain lobbyists put forward what they claim to be scientific evidence, we need to ask ourselves to evaluate these reports critically, ask ourselves who is funding the research, who stands to benefit from the so-called research.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is there a certain narrative or a certain conflict of interest when these lobbyists claim that drugs are safer; when they claim that harm should be reduced; when they take a stance that it is soft on drugs rather than hard on the dangers that they pose to our people and our children?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because tolerating drugs also means tolerating the harm that drugs do to Singaporeans' lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It means tolerating the damage to families − husbands and wives, sons and daughters.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And it also means we have to care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At my Meet-the-People Sessions, I have met young mothers, trying to find work − very difficult.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Juggling looking after their children, trying to find a job, husband in prison because of drugs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met middle-aged men, released from prison.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Looking for employment, trying to rebuild their lives and families.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So that even as we protect our borders from the scourge of drugs, even as we protect our fellow Singaporeans, those hurt by drugs and their families still can find their way to a better future.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, first, I would like to thank the hon Members who proposed this Motion.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It has allowed me to learn a lot and to understand people on the drug issues.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And I agree with the Members on the need to be even more proactive in dealing with drug problems in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to pay tribute to officers in CNB for the work that they do in keeping Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our officers often place their personal safety on the line in the course of their work and I think we ought to put on record our appreciation for their sacrifice and bravery.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This Motion covers three important points but I will only address two of them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The first one on the Motion of applying tough laws to deter drug trafficking into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The second one would be my suggestion for rehabilitative work with drug offenders, traffickers and users alike.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is against my own personal philosophy that I do not believe in a life for another life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Ian Callinan, a former Australian High Court Judge says, "The criminal justice system is fallible.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Any system that retains the death penalty will inevitably, even if infrequently, cause an innocent person to die.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not within our capability to avoid the possibility of error.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In my experience, the phenomenon of human fallibility is irrefutable and, in my view, must be accorded primacy when weighing the arguments in favour of, and against, the death penalty." Sir, any criminal justice system in the world, however advanced, will make mistakes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not a question of having professional, honest and upright judges, Police officers, prosecutors or defence lawyers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However much trust we have in our system, however much faith we have in the people that operate our system, mistakes are unavoidable because humans do make mistakes and, sometimes, genuine mistakes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In a capital case, once the execution takes place and the life of a person is terminated, any mistakes made cannot be corrected.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And as the saying goes, "You can release innocent people from prison, but you cannot release them from their graves".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The criminal justice system has itself demonstrated that it is never 100% sure that the person it is sending to the gallows is, in fact, guilty.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In normal cases, our criminal justice system requires a person's guilt to be proven beyond reasonable doubt before he or she can be convicted and, in the context of capital cases, sentenced to death.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The law has always made it clear that "proof beyond reasonable doubt" does not mean proof beyond all doubt.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But because the death penalty is irreversible, nothing less than proof beyond all doubt would suffice if we are serious about ensuring that no innocent person is wrongfully executed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The answer to me is that, no, we cannot.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But the Court of Appeal was not unanimous.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: On top of this, there are various procedures within the criminal process, which increases the probability of wrongful executions that can happen or may happen.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, accused persons have to instead prove that they are innocent, and they have to do this without the resources available to the Police.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Hor has also pointed out that where there is no access to counsel immediately upon arrest, which could affect the ability of the accused person to defend himself against a capital charge, especially since incriminatory statements obtained by the Police can form the sole basis of conviction, without corroborating or supporting evidence of any kind.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: While there is, indeed, a rule that involuntary statements are inadmissible, proof of exactly what happened in the interrogation room and of exactly how statements are obtained depends entirely on witness testimony of the Police and the accused.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There is no requirement of recording of any kind, even where no defence counsel is present.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Miscarriages of justice have been found in systems, such as Canada, Australia, Norway and many others.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why should we think the situation in Singapore is any different?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, one may ask: have there been any proven cases?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe the right question is whether we should wait until someone is wrongfully executed before we decide to change our position.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: While we do not see it, the reality is that our criminal punishment, especially the death penalty, creates a new class of victims in the families of the death row inmates.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They found themselves having their loved ones taken away from them through no fault of their own.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Most of them are mothers and sisters who have done all that they can to make a decent living for themselves and their families.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In a conversation with a former death row convict who was acquitted by our Court of Appeal, I was struck by the poignancy of how he described the impact of the death penalty on his family.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He told me this, "When you sentence me to death, you sentence my family to death too".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But just as it is important to recognise and address the impact of drugs on the families of drug abusers, I hope we also consider how capital punishment impacts the families of the condemned.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Both groups of family members are equal victims in this process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let us also not forget that the reality is that the ones who are being severely punished are largely the drug mules.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Drug kingpins that operate beyond our borders, who are well sheltered through a complex network chain, are not going to be the ones personally affected by the harsh drug laws put in place and will continue to send individuals, who are often desperate, to supply drugs into our country.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As such, would the death penalty for drug trafficking yield only a slightly higher deterrent effect than alternative punishments?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let us be clear here − drugs are a menace to our society and its use should be eliminated as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let us also not ignore the fact that the question of drug use is not just a criminal justice issue but a social, political and economic one.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, the issue of supply needs to be addressed through the demand lens as well, which I agree with the Members.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We should also be mindful that many traffickers themselves battle addiction, poverty, unemployment and mental illnesses.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In many cases, as recognised by our Courts, they are simply people driven to desperate measures to earn money for their families.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They, too, are ordinary people who have fallen through the cracks and are equally capable of rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not an illness that can be remedied through medication.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is mental, emotional and then it affects the physical being.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Once, my company, Drama Box, did a work with inmates in a DRC.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, in the work there, what struck us most was their concern, the inmates' concern, of how to find a good support system when they move back to society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In one performance when we moved the play out of the DRC and had it performed by performance actors, an audience member from the public shared his experience of how he helped his relative out of the drug problem.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He sent this relative who just left the DRC to work in a logging firm in Brunei, deep in the forest.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Over there, the relative learned about discipline which took him away at the same time from his previous social circle.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When the relative came back to Singapore three years later, he had enough money to start his business.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The rehabilitative process is a very, very long one.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Visual artist Ms Shirley Soh, who worked with some women drug offenders in her Seeing (from) The Other, a work for the Singapore Biennale 2013, noted this, and I quote, "The most important challenging work with the women inmates was to encourage self- expressions in discovering their own stories of growth, change, inspiration and agency that were equally crucial for these women, many of whom had very low self-esteem and were often poorly educated." At the end of the process, Shirley noted, "Ultimately, what surprised the women inmates was how much the art process was about life and their own life experience and aspirations that were worthy of sharing with the outside world." I saw a performance performed by inmates in the prison centre just last year.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It was one of the most beautiful performances I had ever seen.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The sincerity and commitment, but importantly, when you look at the faces and hear the voices of these inmates, when they first appear on stage, slightly embarrassed but as the performance went on, you know that the experience of working on the performance had made them stronger, more confident, more aware of themselves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For this to happen, it really needs the Prison Service to be able to invite more of these works.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we can look at more of such co-operation as proposed by fellow Members, and, of course, managing the process to allow artists to work with these inmates.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, if they are very talented and want to do so, we will be so happy to have more additions to our artistic and creative community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not cast in stone and, just as I hope Members who disagree with me would keep an open mind in this discourse, I, in turn, promise to keep an open mind to any new arguments or evidence that my hon friends and other members of society may bring forward.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I sincerely hope that the Government would do more to facilitate a more informed public discourse on this subject.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I hope to continue this conversation with Members in this House and with my fellow Singaporeans at large.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Deputy Speaker, I would like to first share some stories which I have come to observe and witness first-hand while serving the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The first story was when I was serving as a grassroots leader in Ulu Pandan.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I remember I was still a tertiary student in my second year in University and I was at a Meet-the-People-Session (MPS).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It was a very eye-opening experience for me in general but there was this one story that I will always remember and have repeatedly shared.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One night, a young mother came with her children, very young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The family had not the financial means, the money, to buy the daily supplies that they needed; that is because the husband, the father of the young children, was a drug addict; he could not hold down jobs, could not even start a job.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The young mother, because of her young children, had no choice but to stay around to take care of them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She could not go out to work and, yet, because of the circumstances, they had no savings, no income, no nothing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They managed to somehow make their way, probably by borrowing money, to the MPS to ask for help because of the bills, the arrears, the debts that they had built up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fellow volunteers and I were very struck by this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of the volunteers immediately took the kids to the McDonald's outlet nearby to buy them a simple meal, so that they can have a full stomach.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The rest, some of us stayed back to write letters of appeal and try to find different ways to help her solve her financial distress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That was something that I walked away with, thinking about it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the Government, as a society, there are many things that we can do to help them but, in the end, if someone has been taken down by drugs because drugs have poisoned this person, this person is no longer functioning normally, what we see is a debilitating effect on the innocent lives of people around them, their loved ones, the young ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To date, it is something that still sticks with me.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even within the current community that I serve, I have also met quite a number of drug abusers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A number of them, at least two men I have met, after abusing drugs, even though they are now back in the community, they still suffer psychosis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are unable to be self-reliant, they are unable to hold down jobs, they have to rely on their siblings or their elderly parents, really aged parents, to still help them, to subsist them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Again, we try to give them financial assistance but there is only so much that we can do.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Here we are, we see two able-bodied men basically unable to do anything more productive than just living the days out.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As shared by hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza, we have all seen the photos and the videos that went viral sometime last year in the United States where young toddlers were left to fend for himself or herself at the backseat of the car because the parents were overdosed on drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Another one, a little toddler, just sitting next to her mother who had had collapsed because of heroin overdose; just crying, so lonely, so helpless.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a parent and as any responsible parent in this House and outside of this House, we can all agree that such scenes are simply heartbreaking and we would not want to see it on our own children or, for that matter, on any other child out there because we feel for them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are real stories of how drugs destroy the lives of those who abuse them and of the innocent people around them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Illicit drugs remain a scourge of all societies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is like a voracious vortex pulling family members and the community in a downward spiral.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Real harm is inflicted upon the abuser, his family and the wider community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, I can never really understand how the choice of certain individuals in wanting to use illicit drugs can be allowed to destroy the lives and future of so many innocent people out there.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We know that drugs destroy families in drug-tolerant countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many people started experimenting with illicit drugs to satisfy their curiosity towards the perceived thrill and exhilaration.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Often, it is also a result of peer pressure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, because of the insidious nature of such addictive drugs, users who thought they were just using drugs recreationally may find themselves unable to escape addiction.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Worse, the diminishing effects of illicit drug abuse drives the abuser to consume a greater amount each time just to achieve that same euphoric sensation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And if they do not get that "fix", they suffer terrible withdrawal symptoms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This means that more and more money is needed to finance the drug habit.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This can lead to financial exhaustion and, more tragically, death from drug overdose.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is not uncommon to hear the sad plight of families when the sole breadwinner becomes entangled with illicit drug and is addicted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Sometimes, families of drug abusers find themselves trapped in huge debt taken to feed the abuser's drug habit.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The families are constantly harassed by creditors and, more heartbreakingly, families get broken up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The most pitiful victims are none other than children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is 2.2 million lives that we are talking about.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we are not careful, such heartwrenching scenes as the ones that we have described about toddlers being left alone to fend for themselves, or even like the little toddler in pink pyjamas sitting there crying next to her mother who had collapsed, will become commonplace in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Illicit drugs can creep in insidiously and poison young lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza shared a lot of statistics on drugs and the situation of drugs in Singapore and how drug use among youths is at risk of creeping up further.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Youths are especially vulnerable because, at an adolescent age, they are still developing judgement and decision-making skills.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some get the wrong impression that taking drugs can help to enhance athletic performance or ease anxiety problems.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some are impressionable and give in to peer pressure to feel accepted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What is also very worrying is that based on reports from the National Library of Medicine, young people appear to move more quickly through the stages towards addiction than adults.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In today's context, it is no longer youths with disadvantaged family backgrounds who abuse illicit drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are now more cases of youths from privileged backgrounds experimenting with illicit drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is supported by the findings in the World Drug Report 2016 that individuals belonging to higher socio-economic groups tend to have a greater propensity to initiate drug use than lower socio-economic groups.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, with growing affluence and connectivity to the Internet, there are now more available options to obtain drugs online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Being Internet-savvy, some youths are able to obtain illicit drugs through the Internet called the "Dark-Net".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The "Dark-Net" is a remote part of the Internet which is often used for illegal activities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It has been reported that these websites even offer free samples to bait curious youths into experimenting, knowing fully well that the return on investment from giving a free sample is a very high chance of addiction and subsequent demand for drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, with the perceived "anonymity" of the Internet, youths may be less fearful of obtaining illicit drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With all interactions made virtually, without physical interactions with the drug traffickers and usage of sophisticated cashless transactions, like bitcoin, youths may feel more at ease to obtain drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: An update to the global survey in 2016 showed an increase in users obtaining drugs using online platforms, of which the United Kingdom has the highest rate of novel psychoactive substance purchased among the countries surveyed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What is also startling is that 5% of respondents stated that they did not consume drugs prior to accessing them through these online platforms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This may be low level compared with other countries, but its rapid rise is the one that should worry us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, we must ensure that our laws and enforcement are kept up to date to prevent our Singaporeans, especially our young Singaporeans, from getting their hands on drugs via the Internet.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have also talked about drug addiction continuing to be a clear and present danger, especially with the emergence of online sources.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To combat the scourge of drug abuse, we need to focus our concerted efforts on education, deterrence and rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To be clear, I hope nobody will ever need to be subjected to such stiff penalties because that will mean that everyone is healthy and is leading a full and happy life but, given how addictive drugs are, hoping for that is simply wishful thinking.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need tough laws and penalties to act as a powerful deterrent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition to creating stiffer deterrence, I have also mentioned how rehabilitation and education are equally important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to bear in mind that there are still Singaporeans who have fallen prey to the poison of drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must rehabilitate them and help them to reintegrate into society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Successful rehabilitation outcomes often depend on the drug user's tenacity and resilience in staying in treatment long enough to reap its full benefits.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is also important that we help drug users to eventually reintegrate into society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must help former drug offenders battle the demons of addiction through strong community support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The phrase "prevention is better than cure" holds a lot of truth, especially in our fight against drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is in a way strengthening mental resilience, conditioning them to be stronger.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Members of this House are aware of the harmful effects that drugs can cause to the live of an individual and to society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a mother of a 20-month-old toddler, every day, as I watch him grow, as he learns new words, learns new things and the excitement that he derives when he gets praised for little achievements, I rejoice with him.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is my greatest desire and wish to see him succeed in life, to see that he has a healthy life, that he is able to pursue his aspirations and make the best out of the time that he has in this life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe that all parents out there wish the same for their children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And so, I feel a sense of responsibility – and, indeed, I think so, too, the Members in this House and members of society out there – that we must make sure that we create the most conducive environment for our younger generation so that they can grow up with the right values, with good health and have the best opportunities to go forth in their lives and pursue their dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I would like to echo my support to go towards a 100% drug-free Singapore − one that does not tolerate drugs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I stand in full support of the Motion.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I will focus specifically on the call to invest in drug rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Frankly, I am not that well-versed on the drug issue.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, to prepare to speak on this Motion, I talked to former hard-core drug addicts, as well as people in the social sector who have been helping to rebuild their lives, post-incarceration.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, consequently, many of them have seen friends fall back to taking drugs and going back into prison.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I asked them what they personally thought of Singapore's laws on drugs and one former hard-core drug addict put it this way, "The laws are tough and cruel but it is necessary.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we get a lighter sentence, no second thoughts, sure go back to drugs." The recovering addicts were not naive about the depths of self-destruction they were willing to go through to feed the beast within.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They had come to accept the need for tough rules to help them draw boundaries on their behaviours.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I asked them and social workers for insights about what could help former addicts stick to the straight and narrow path of rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I will list the top five issues they brought up, as well as their requests and proposed solutions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The tough reality for many recovering addicts when they exit prison is that they may not have family or friends willing to give them a home.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They often lack financial resources to purchase a flat and while the option of rental flats is open to them, the waiting list is long.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: As a consequence, many have no home to go to and end up staying way longer than they expected in halfway houses.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One former drug addict said, "I have many friends who are stuck in halfway houses.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of them are in their 40s and 50s and still working as a house remover.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: How long can they do house removing jobs considering their age?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
