text: If they have their own house, maybe they can move on and explore various career paths." Feeling like you are in personal and professional limbo for too long can be really demoralising and actually raise the risk of these ex-offenders backsliding back to addiction for comfort.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But easier access to rental housing is only one part of the issue because, even for those who do get one, there is another problem.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Without a community of accountability around them, when one roommate falls back into drugs or crime, it is not uncommon to hear of the other roommate rapidly following suit.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, this simple problem of unstable housing without a supportive community can thus potentially erase years of costly investment into the rehabilitation process.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We need to invest in an innovative public housing solution for our ex-offenders that marries the system of accountability of halfway houses together with the space to live independently within society.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is already a great model in the social sector that we could learn from − the AWWA Senior Community Home in Ang Mo Kio is Singapore's first seniors' home embedded within two levels of an existing HDB rental block.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is the only one of its kind and only one of its scale, housing 140 people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It has been around since 1976 and is one of the most inspiring public housing innovations I have seen here.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Two to three seniors live in each 1-room rental flat and interspersed in the units, are purpose-built spaces like recreation rooms, laundry rooms, nursing stations and a community kitchen.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It even once explored having a retail space for the seniors to sell their products.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This holistic housing solution has allowed people without family support to live within an existing HDB neighbourhood, affirming they still have a place in society, while preserving their desire for independence and providing a supportive community to look out for their needs.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope HDB can consider partnering with VWOs with an established track record of rehabilitating ex-offenders to pilot a smaller scale community home.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Like the AWWA example, the prototype community home could zone out a few floors in an HDB rental block for ex-offenders to have housing, a supportive programming and a system of strong accountability, all rolled into one.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The second most brought-up issue was on the effects of long-term imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: While the social workers and recovering addicts understood the punitive need for tough laws, they maintained that these long periods of incarceration also produced significant social side-effects that undermined the rehabilitation process.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Extended and repeated periods of incarceration are a time of great vulnerability for offenders and their families, and it is during this time that spouses grow apart, divorce happens and children start to exhibit even more dysfunctional and distancing behaviours.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: On top of that, given the speed of change in Singapore, five to seven years in prison is a very long time for someone to be taken out of market.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, those who get incarcerated younger have a better chance of making something of their lives.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But for mid-life offenders who emerge out of prison in their late 40s to 50s, their relevance and marketability of skills would have significantly diminished.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: To come out of prison to such personal and professional failure again is crushing and some do turn back to drugs and return to prison because they feel they really have nothing left to lose.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If the length of incarceration is a non-negotiable due to the first objective of security, then can we consider investing in a lot more targeted rehab solutions for long-term prisoners to help them achieve the second and third objectives of deterrence?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We must increase the outreach and frequency of family-bonding programmes that help keep parent-child relations resilient throughout the long period of incarceration.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is the VWO New Life Stories where volunteers help incarcerated mothers record themselves telling bed-time stories so that their pre-schooling kids can listen to it at home and maintain connection.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the Reading with Dads programme run by the Centre for Fathering.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In the first run in Changi Prison, eight fathers had the rare chance to just sit on the floor with their kids and hug them and read books with them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One of them, a father of five shared that it was the happiest day of his life and it was like a dream.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Grown men were crying − and I am not talking just about the inmates − but the prison officers watching.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We should also consider investing more in arts-based programmes as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think enough credit is given to how the arts does do deeply healing work, helping people surface the deep stories and emotions that do lie beneath their behaviours.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One arts educator who works with prisons told me of a young offender who told her very sternly, "Madam, don't ever stop this programme.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I kena rotan many times I never cry.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But in your class, I cry because you make me feel something again." In our line of empathy-building work, I can tell you tears are one of the most powerful KPIs we pay attention to because they tell you something in the heart has shifted.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A lot of change can happen in five to seven years, especially for prisoners with young children.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Incarcerated parents, fathers especially, must be given more bonding time, so that both parents and children do not lose faith that they are still wanted and still loved.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The last thing we want is for kids to grow up motherless or fatherless, which, in turn, increases the next generation's risk of falling into similar patterns of drug abuse and incarceration.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is much we can gain if we invest in creative, innovative programmes that help to rebuild trust between long-term prisoners and their families.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The third issue they raised was length of detention time spent in halfway houses.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The fourth issue is the lack of publicly available statistics on rehab issues.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is a desire among halfway houses and other VWOs involved in rehab work to design better solutions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: However, many of them are going only by a mix of gut instincts or learned experience.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They do not have the resources to commission or conduct base-line research into how well various rehabilitation efforts and programmes are working out in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Fresh and openly available data will help us better figure out what is working, what is not working and where change is most needed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The last issue has to do with quality of in-prison education programmes.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I saved this for last because I wanted to end this on a strong affirmation to Singapore Prisons that there is much good being done on this front.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Prisoners actually love the learning and employment opportunities they have been getting.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many look forward to the academic, vocational training and arts-based programmes that have been brought in.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, the issue here is more of a happy one.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They say, "Can we have more of the good stuff please?" We should encourage their hunger to learn.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I asked ex-offenders for vocational training programme suggestions and one of the most intriguing suggestions I got was this: "Why can't we train up more ex-offenders to take leadership in halfway houses?" This was his brutally honest take: "Social workers in this field are not effective at all.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A drug addict only listens to a drug addict.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Halfway house leaders must be an ex-convict, not just a highly educated psychologist." I personally believe there is definitely still a place for educated social workers and psychologists at halfway houses.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What was once the ex-offender's greatest weakness on his resume − his experiences of incarceration and addiction − could then become his unique asset.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I also want to flag up the voice of another key stakeholder in the rehab process: external vendors who run programmes in prison.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The best of them love the charges that they work with and are deeply passionate about partnering with Singapore Prisons to work on the rehab process.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That is why some of them struggle greatly with seeing how the GeBIZ procurement process sometimes ends up awarding programmes to the lowest bidder or a new bidder for the sake of trying out a new vendor.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some share that it hurts to see meaningful projects gaining ground with the inmates get derailed simply because of what they saw as a procurement process.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They felt that contracts sometimes ended up going to vendors that did not have a genuine interest in rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Those who do rehab work seriously do not want to be treated or accessed as short-term vendors but rather long-term partners in a healing process.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: These programming providers believe that it is counter-productive to put high-stakes human-centric programmes at the mercy of an open call tender on GeBIZ.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But I also believe we will gain more ground in the fight against drugs when we become equally known for the things we are for, rather than just known for the things we are against.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It challenges us to hold both punitive justice and restorative mercy in tension.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is a difficult position but I believe it is also the most useful way forward.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I say so not based on theory but because that is how I have seen it play out in the transformed lives of people I know who have done their time in prison and walked down that hard road of rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our former drug abusers can be so much more than their past mistakes.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Preparing to speak on this Motion actually reminded me that I happen to be friends with a few recovering addicts and ex-offenders.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It took me a moment to remember because I had long gotten used to just seeing them as loving husbands and kind fathers, humble pastors and compassionate counsellors, successful entrepreneurs and talented creatives.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen the evidence of investment in rehabilitation in ordinary lives.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is arduous and it is costly but it works.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is gold in each of us, even the worst of us, that can be revealed through grace.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Let us do what we can to help our recovering addicts stay connected to their families and their hopes for the future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Deputy Speaker, the recent United Nations Committee on Narcotic Drugs (CND) meeting in Vienna in the middle of March threw up several interesting perspectives on how the East and the West view drugs and laws regarding its consumption and trafficking.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Drug trafficking is a multi-billion dollar global illicit trade.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This dependence on drugs places a heavy burden not only on the individual but also their loved ones, public healthcare systems and security agencies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At that same meeting, it was galling to note the nonchalance towards the drug menace displayed by some countries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some European countries took turns to conflate drug use with human rights.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same conference, Russia talked about compulsory drug tests for teenagers while the US and Canada talked about reconciling the legislation and legalisation of marijuana with UN's drug conventions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Canada and Uruguay even spent long hours discussing the important issue of quotas for how marijuana bushes should be allowed to be grown per household!

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are those who justify that softening the drug stance is because current drug control policies are failing and the rising numbers of drug consumers − you cannot even call them addicts anymore − drug consumers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I say, just because your system has failed does not mean your next solution is something everyone else should accept.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our streets are safe from drugs and crime.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And, so, I add my voice to the many Members, including the hon Member, Mr Christopher de Souza, in calling on the Government to continue to apply tough laws to deter drug trafficking into Singapore and combating the scourge of drugs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we are relatively safe from drugs, I am still worried.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The idea of soft drugs, as many Members have mentioned, recreational drugs, as some people call them, I think we must acknowledge drugs cause harm, whether they are soft or hard, whatever name you call it, they are drugs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You look at programmes, you look at drama series from overseas, the glamorisation of a lifestyle filled with drugs, perhaps that is affecting mindsets as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The increase in the number of new drug users attests to this as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I do not believe there is a difference between hard drugs and soft drugs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They both cause harm and should be prevented with equal measure and equal vigour.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our open data age, availability of drugs online and its ease of shipment are something we should really be concerned about.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many have spoken about the Dark Net and, therefore, I hope that the Government will be able to look more at the measures to stem this rot to prevent more younger Singaporeans from taking the easy route in obtaining drugs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another cause for concern is the trafficking and consumption of synthetic drugs, including stimulants like amphetamine, methamphetamine and ecstasy-types of substances.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although some say that they are not considered as dangerous as heroin or cocaine, sustained consumption still causes damage to oneself and loved ones.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of us would have come across drug addicts, drug abusers in our communities and the damage that it causes to them and their health, as well as to their families.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, we should have more prevention and education measures, especially for our young, to stem the tide of synthetic drugs as well and tighten the regulations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is important that there is just punishment for those who traffick drugs for those who use drugs that they have an opportunity to recover.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While I urge the Government to be firm in maintaining deterrence, I also believe that justice must be tempered with mercy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many traffickers, for example, are far down the hierarchy of crime syndicates and some are forced by circumstances.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the trap doors open, the absoluteness of this punishment cannot be turned back.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When you look at the jurisdictions that mandate the death penalty for drug crimes, I think we can also conclude that it is not just the threat of capital punishment that prevents drug trafficking and reduces drug crime in a country.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I also, therefore, urge the Government to do more to rehabilitate our drug addicts and free them from this new form of slavery.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of them are wounded by circumstances or bad choices in life and, therefore, the most important reassurance we can give to them is that they have a place at the table, that they are not abandoned by society, cast aside because of a bad choice.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the recent Narcotics: Problems and Solutions of this Global Issue Conference, Pope Francis was the keynote speaker, he said, "Every addicted person brings with them a distinct personal history, which should be listened to, understood, loved, and, where possible, cured.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Examples, such as Asher Quek, who recovered from an early life of drugs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: His first encounter with drugs was at the age of 13, spent time in prison.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But because he was inspired and challenged by counsellors in prison, he now volunteers himself as a counsellor to other drug abusers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This perhaps is one example of how a good rehabilitation and support system can work.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But in 2014, I met three young children in my estate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One very young girl, just started Primary 1, her brother was in Primary 2 and older sister was in Secondary 1.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I met them because their uncle came to approach me, asking for a job.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I realised that these three children were not his.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Probing deeper, it was revealed that their parents, both mother and father, were incarcerated because of drug offences.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The older sister took it upon herself to look after her younger siblings.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although the mother is out of prison today, she feels and suffers from withdrawal symptoms and we do what we can.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the thing that really inspires her is her younger daughter who has never given up on her parents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And when I last met them, she simply said to me, "There are many things I love in life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Sweet red watermelons and my parents, whatever they have done." Family support is important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A society that accepts them for their weaknesses is important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A society that tempers justice with mercy is also important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What works elsewhere would not necessarily work here.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we must continue to do more to break the supply chain, ensure that we do not go soft on drug use, reminding our young Singaporeans that drugs have a tremendous negative impact on them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: An addictions specialist − his name was Dr Munidasa Winslow − recently noted that an increase has happened in clients buying drugs on the Internet and receiving them by postal mail.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would, however, Sir, like to add a note of caution when it comes to young Singaporean offenders.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They deserve not only to be seen through the battle-hardened prosecutor's lens of specific deterrence, but also with a keen eye towards rehabilitation, which is why I am happy that rehabilitation is also a part of this particular Motion.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This Motion has been characterised as involving different imperatives.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza spoke of the importance of law and order; of weeding out a transnational scourge: drug addiction; of having muscular laws.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, young first-time drug offenders deserve to be treated fairly and, in appropriate cases, compassionately as well.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is the duty of the sentencing judge in a Misuse of Drugs Act case to assess and balance these competing concerns and to strike an appropriate balance between the two.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the final analysis, the public interest to be tough on drug crimes and the interests of young first-time offenders are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Our Courts give special regard to cases involving young offenders and it is about this that I would like to speak about today.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: First, I recall that as early as in 1999, the Singapore High Court held that, in cases of a young first-time offender, there can rarely be any conflict between his interest and that of the public's.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The public have no greater interest than that he become a good citizen.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: A decade ago, I had the privilege of being the defence co-counsel in one such case.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We represented Mr Ridzuan bin Hanafi on a pro bono basis against his charge of trafficking 20 tablets of ecstasy.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: A 20-year-old NSF at that time, Ridzuan took responsibility for his mistake.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We met his family at the hawker centre where his mother ran a nasi campur stall.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We learned that Ridzuan's eldest sister had been diagnosed with cancer and that, to supplement his NSF stipend, he worked two other odd jobs.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: His unwavering care and support for his family was clear.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He saved this money prudently and contributed in whatever way he could.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: After realising that this was not enough to take care of his sister, he slipped.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: His heart was set on equipping himself to provide a good future for himself and his family.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Despite not having completed his course of study at ITE, he had expressed a genuine wish to further his studies in the field of audio engineering upon completion of National Service.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ridzuan then obtained a deferment and enrolled in the Singapore Audio Engineering Institute.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As a filial son to his mum, Ridzuan's greatest concern had been to ensure that his ageing mother, who has sacrificed the better part of her life to take care of her children, did not have to continue to work so hard at her nasi campur stall and, therefore, jeopardise her health as well in supporting herself and her daughter.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ridzuan loathed the idea of depending on his mother and his family.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He confessed to selling the ecstasy pills for cash and we learnt all of this from several visits to his home, to Queenstown Remand Prison, where he was also serving pre-trial detention at the place and we asked in Court for probation as the appropriate sentence for the sentencing judge to consider and to sentence him.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When determining whether or not an order of probation is required or appropriate, a sentencing judge may call for a pre-sentence or probation report, as the judge did in Ridzuan's case.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: A probation report provides a comprehensive profile of the offender and is obtained mainly from interviews with the offender, his family, significant people which, in this case, included people he was working with in National Service, his superior officers, social service agencies and so on.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It gives a picture of that drug offender so that the drug offender is not just a digit, not just one person accused of a crime of consumption or trafficking, but there is a larger contextual, social and historical nature to the offence and the offender.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It provides the Court with an alternative method of dealing with that first-time young offender who may otherwise have to be committed to a corrective penal institution.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It involves the conditional suspension of punishment when the offender is released under supervision and the personal care of a probation officer.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: A probation order imposes on the probationer certain obligations in the form of conditions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ridzuan's Probation Officer found his family members were willing and stable to assist in his rehabilitation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: His youngest sister was willing to defer her overseas education just to take care of him.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Probation Officer also looked at the unwavering reports from his superiors in National Service.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The prosecution, of course, appealed against this decision at that time.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I draw attention to this not because the prosecutors were doing something wrong.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It was their job to appeal against it because it was the first time probation had been awarded against a drug trafficking charge.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But I take issue with the way in which the sentence and the offender were characterised.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the Magistrate's Appeal, this is what the prosecutors said and these were their words, not mine, Mr Deputy Speaker: "The drug menace still abounds in Singapore even though our drug laws are enforced vigorously.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Drug trafficking is the scourge of our society, family and the individual drug abuser.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As such, peddlers in this evil trade must be dealt with severely to alert those in this pernicious enterprise that they too will be prosecuted and punished severely." By itself, there is not something too greatly wrong with that paragraph.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But the next paragraph is stark: "  has a dismal academic track record.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He shows excessive indulgence in clubbing, has sold cigarettes in his army camp to his friends in order to support his clubbing habit.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There is hardly any evidence that he has a bright future ahead of him unless a fledging interest in sound engineering (which is a euphemism for being a music disc-jockey) constitutes a potentially sound career or a safe life choice that would not throw him back into the clubbing culture." This was how the prosecution had characterised him.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It would be the investigators and everybody who was part of the criminal justice system looking at one young first-time drug offender who was standing before them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I take issue with this, Mr Deputy Speaker, with conflating the crime, as reprehensible as it may be, with the prospects of the young offender.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, once you label a crime as being "evil", it is a short step before you demonise the criminal as well, regardless of his young age.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Should the young offender's prospects of reform and rehabilitation be a foregone conclusion that prosecutors alone can make?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We must be wary, Mr Deputy Speaker, of what the Judge of Appeal Chao Hick Tin cautioned just last month in a case that Mr Kok Heng Leun referred to earlier.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Both of them were acquitted after lengthy trials.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: How will young potential offenders be better encouraged to abstain from resorting to drugs in the first place and before the criminal justice system itself is involved?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Two, how should options for rehabilitation, including but not limited to the drug rehabilitation centre, be approached?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I note that Mr Christopher de Souza has some very intelligent ideas in the paper that he has provided.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If there were refinements to the Misuse of Drugs Act, could we also involve lawyers who have represented these young first-time drug offenders from the Law Society, from the Association of Criminal Lawyers and other organisations and law firms?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will we be able to invite social workers and probation officers to also be involved in how these amendments are being included or proposals being put forward?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will they be required to spend time conversing with under-privileged people and those who are most prone to substance abuse?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to conclude by saying that as we examine the Motion which asks us to think harder on being tough against drug crimes, we must also think of humanising those people who are drug offenders, especially those who are young, first-time Singaporean drug offenders.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I support the Motion and hope that the hon proposer as well as the Ministry will take these comments into consideration as the law is amended.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But maybe, I will just add a few brief points.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am glad that in this House, we have not really had a debate on one issue and, that is, the seriousness of the drug threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Everyone here has agreed that drugs are a menace and we have to find a way to deal with it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Before we look at what we want to change, I think we need to look at what Singapore has done well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a percentage of the population, I believe it is below 0.001% of the population.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, if we look at the latest UNODC report, it said one in 20 people in the world has used drugs and that translates into a quarter of a billion people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if you talk about overall statistics, Singapore is doing very well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My own view – and I suspect this is shared by many others in the House – is that this is not because of any one measure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is no silver bullet, but rather the suite of measures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if we look at the big picture, I think Singapore is doing a good job in its fight against drugs and the low incidence of drug rates contrast favourably with many other countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, the rates of drugs are so low that many people may not even have encountered drug addicts in their lives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My first encounter was after I started as a Member of Parliament and I met a gentleman who came to the Meet-the-People Session (MPS) who was telling me very badly why he needed cough mixture.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I did not really understand why he was having difficulty getting cough mixture until he told me that he had actually been banned from buying cough mixture and his name was with several doctors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That was when I realised, as he told me more and more, he also asked me to write a letter to excuse him from urine tests.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As I spoke to him more, his thoughts were disjointed but, basically, it finally emerged that he was actually an addict and he was an addict who had served his sentence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: He had come out but he was in danger of re-offending and very likely had re-offended which is why he did not want to go for his upcoming urine test.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Later on that evening, he brought his wife along to help make the argument for him.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But when he moved away, his wife said, "please make sure that he does not get any more cough mixture." So, it is quite clear the families of addicts suffer along with the addicts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But there were many more stories after that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my community, we have a programme where we reach out to ex-offenders just before their release from prison.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And one of the things that strikes me is that ex-offenders who have the biggest difficulty coming back in are those who have drug antecedents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are also the ones who are most likely to have offended before and to have committed other offences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are the ones that we really have to make a special effort to reach out to, to try and make sure their families still accept them which is also a difficulty because, in some cases, the family is outside, may have divorced the inmate, may have moved on.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are all the challenges that I think drug addicts face.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The biggest issue, of course, is that they became addicts in the first place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think we should do everything we can to prevent that happening and I believe the tough measures we have taken have achieved that effect.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, there are just two points I would address.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not wish to address the whole system, but the two trends of concern that the CNB raised in its latest report.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Cannabis has developed a reputation in some other countries or, at least, it has been marketed in some countries as being a perfectly harmless drug and has been legalised.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would not make the argument Mr Christopher de Souza has made earlier.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think he has quite comprehensively covered the programmes in these countries where it has been legalised and shown that it actually has caused harm.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The tough measures that we have against cannabis are actually generally quite helpful and relevant.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is one additional suggestion I have and I think this also relates to the point about rehabilitation of young offenders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the countries that had a very successful programme on rehabilitating of offenders which we can learn from, I believe, is Iceland.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Between 1998 and 2016, Iceland ran a programme specifically for youths.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was a study of Icelandic youths between the ages of 15 and 16.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First of all, of course, Singapore's figures are nowhere close to these.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We do not have addiction rates of 17%.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it would be quite shocking if we hit that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The point is that we should not adopt everything they have done wholesale, but I think their rehabilitation programmes specifically probably have things that we can learn from.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The main thrust of their programmes involves promoting alternative recreational facilities, strengthening family ties, improving self-sufficiency and building social competency for youths who were identified as being at risk.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand that we have a lot of programmes targeted at this by different agencies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I believe that there might be something useful to learn from these programmes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The main focus of these programmes is to keep at-risk youths occupied, usefully engaged and socially involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, I would like to focus on how we need to improve our rehabilitation process and how we need to strengthen our focus on family support during the rehabilitation process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is almost two-thirds and, if we can improve our rehabilitation process, then we will effectively solve two-thirds of our problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I raised this previously during the COS debates and I said that, and I quote, "A significant focus of the rehabilitation process is to ensure that inmates are able to secure a job when they are released.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I feel that an equally important factor is whether they have family support when they are released." Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin replied that, and I quote, "Singapore Prison Service (SPS) partners with Fei Yue Family Services and Lakeside Family Services to provide structured family programmes for inmates − workshops to help better understand the impact of their crimes on their families and build their parenting and communication skills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Prison Service also works with community partners like Salvation Army to conduct family sessions in prison.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During these sessions, family members are allowed to enter prison to spend time with the inmates and they are designed to encourage bonding between inmates and their children and they serve as powerful reminders to inmates that they need to turn their lives around.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These family sessions are also held during special occasions, such as Mother's Day, Father's Day and Children's Day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Other than helping inmates, Singapore Prison Service also helps their families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The grassroots-led Yellow Ribbon Community Project (YRCP) was established to help the families and children of inmates cope, by connecting them to the national social support networks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They recognised that family ties are vital to inmates' rehabilitation and family support is especially important after the inmates' release, and thus, the community's long-term involvement is vital to ensure continuity in these efforts." We are currently indeed emphasising the important role of family support in rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the statistics show that there is still a problem and there is always room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that additional requests for family visits by DRC inmates or their family members are rare.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The lack of visits by family members is a tell-tale sign that there are problems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the family bond is strong, then, surely, there will be more family visits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Drug consumption might be the symptom of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, while we focus our efforts on tackling the symptom of the problem, we also need to remember to tackle the root of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The lack of strong family bonds might be the reason they consumed drugs in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The other even more worrying statistic is that the more times we incarcerate someone for drug offences, the higher the chances he or she will be incarcerated again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It should be the other way around where the recidivism rate should be higher for someone incarcerated once as compared to someone incarcerated for the fourth time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that one of the reasons for the higher recidivism rate for LT2 inmates is that they find it harder to reintegrate back into society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am certain that one of the other factors is again the lack of family support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I completely understand how difficult it is for family bonds to be strengthened during the rehabilitation process, considering that these bonds would have been further damaged as a result of the incarceration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I completely understand how lost someone must feel when their loved ones are incarcerated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have met many residents who come to my MPS, appealing for help after their loved ones were incarcerated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I recently met a mother of five who had to now single-handedly support the whole family while her husband is in the DRC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was thrown into the deep end and this will not be an easy chapter in her life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I completely understand the immense guilt a drug offender must feel when he or she leaves their family behind to fend for themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to do more to strengthen our rehabilitation process and we need to view the rehabilitation process more holistically and focus on how we can rebuild the broken family bonds and focus on a more family-oriented rehabilitation process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As mentioned earlier, Singapore Prison Service is already providing workshops to help inmates better understand the impact of their crimes on their families and build their parenting and communication skills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, can we do more workshops where it is attended by both the inmate and their spouse or loved ones?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate the possible security and logistics concerns but I believe the pros outweigh the cons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With regard to the family sessions conducted in prison, can we increase the number and duration of such family sessions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is perhaps the most powerful rehabilitation tool.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my earlier speech, I said, and I quote, "I watched fathers in tears as they realised how much they missed their children and perhaps how their actions have hurt their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I saw in the eyes of the fathers a resolve to be rehabilitated so that they can reunite with the children − not just for a day but for the rest of their lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I also saw what that one day meant for the children, as ultimately the children are indeed the real victims." Can we also be more proactive in reaching out to the families and children of inmates?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand from the mother of five children whom I mentioned earlier that nobody reached out to her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is the crucial period and the help we can provide will be essential.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We already recognise the need for family support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are, in fact, individual anti-addiction programmes for ex-offenders at halfway houses, such as HighPoint, Pertapis, Green Haven, just to name a few, and at hospitals, such as the Raffles Counselling Centre and the National Addictions Management Service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These programmes do bring in family support at some stage of the rehabilitation process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the extent to which the family is brought into the rehabilitation process depends on the individual programmes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also requires the ex-offenders taking the initiative to first enrol in these programmes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Taskforce had recommended developing more targeted strategies to address youth drug abuse, such as toolkits for parents, educators, counsellors and NS commanders and introducing rehabilitation programmes for youths.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This led to CNB developing a guide for parents of children recovering from drug abuse titled "Staying Drug-Free".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I must end this speech by saying that I completely understand how disappointing it must be for them when they see a drug offender return to prison again and be under their care repeatedly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It must not be easy for them and I sincerely hope we can help break this cycle, strengthen our rehabilitation process and strengthen family bonds.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This Motion is a timely reminder for us to remain vigilant, continue to be tough on drugs and make this a national priority.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As we debate the way forward, what do we do next?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Others talked about the mood within Singapore, young people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As we assess how we move forward, I think it is useful for Members to understand a little bit about how the history of our fight against drugs evolved and really look at the period between the 1960s and 1980s.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In a snapshot, what did we have then?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We had abusers stealing, committing crimes to feed their addiction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If I give some numbers, I think Members will be shocked and I will give some numbers in a minute.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We saw it as a menace and we said we had to fight it; which is why in every speech I make, I emphasise it is not a single solution, not just the death penalty.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The legislative framework was put in through the MDA in 1973.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And then Operation Ferret was launched to reverse the momentum.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You can guess from the name what it meant.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So CNB, the Police Force, they coordinated their efforts, flushed out the abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we had not done that, the law and order situation today in Singapore that we take for granted would be very different.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, for people outside this House and for the hon Nominated Member of Parliament who advocates a softer approach, suggests that our laws are too tough, remember these figures.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When you do not enforce, you get one picture; and 26,000 people by 1978.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the 1980s, we still had more than 8,000 in DRC.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is where we were and, today, everyone accepts, even The Economist accepts, that we have the drug situation under control, perhaps the only country to be able to say that openly and directly and backed up by the facts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We set up a committee to improve the drug situation in November 1993 with a comprehensive anti-drug strategy − preventive drug education in the schools, tough laws backed up by tough enforcement, rehabilitation, aftercare.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have had a good run for 20 years but now consider the global situation and how that might impact on us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That probably does not include the type of cases that Mr Christopher de Souza talked about, where people under the influence of drugs caused traffic accidents and killed others.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are people who died as a result of drug abuse − 200,000.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh is right that global conversation is about a softer stance on drugs, seductive arguments using pseudo-science and glamorising drugs, and they do create a challenging environment for us to keep Singapore drug-free.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at the evidence, you look at the US, opioid abuse, the prescriptions went up three-fold since 1999, fuelled by people relying on and accepting questionable evidence that these are benign pain remedies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Going into diversions and misuse, thousands get hooked on to it, and then guess what happens?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, New York Times reported that there were 33,000 deaths per year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For those with bleeding hearts who talk about inmates on death row, I think they should think about these 33,000 deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Why not spend some time with them rather than just crying with the people in the death row?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is, as Mr Christopher de Souza pointed out, a trafficker engaging in a crime of cynicism or crime with cynicism for profit.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He knows what he is doing, he is coming in for money and there is nothing on the spur about it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The same arguments that were used to try and get opium allowed are now being used for cannabis legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The arguments, if you look at them, are evocative but little clinical evidence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is some suggestion – Mr Pritnam Singh talked about it, others talked about it – about how people are now going into medical marijuana and medical cannabis and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I said at the United Nations I do not want human rights groups preaching to me about the medical value of cannabis.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If a respectable medical association is prepared to tell me that this ought to be prescribed as medicine, we will look at it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That there is no proven record for this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There can be no objection to any substance being prescribed by a doctor based on scientific evidence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think there is every objection to a blanket legislation allowing free use of cannabis or opium on the basis of some questionable medical suggestion which no medical association worth its salt is prepared to back up.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh is right: legalisation around the world is gaining ground.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He quoted Malaysia, Thailand and Israel, but my point is, a large majority of Singaporeans stand by what is right, stand by our position.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Even internationally, when I went to the UN, we brought along a doctor who had pored through a substantial amount of medical literature on substance abuse, cannabis abuse, in particular, and was prepared to stand up and present that this is the impact cannabis has on your brain structure and it makes you dependent.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Science is always evolving and if science evolves to a different stage, we are practical people and we rely on facts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza pointed out how drug abuse has worsened in Colorado since they legalised cannabis.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Even when we go to these international conferences, the NGOs which support legalisation come out with brochures which are glitzy, which are very attractive, evocative.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are all financed by the pharma companies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, after having lost tens of thousands of lives, they move to focusing on public health issues, HIV.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you get an alliance with a commercial interest and countries saying we cannot handle this anymore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are now saying let us create a new international norm.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Well, I do not have a problem if they change their rules; but I do have a problem if they want to change international norms and say every country should follow that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In order to get its stuff on to the West, sometimes or quite often, they seem to want to take the road through Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are a major transport hub, 200 million people go through our airport, shores, land checkpoints.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because of the wealth factor, our people can pay, therefore, it is an attractive destination, both for transhipment and as a destination source.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second major challenge is drug peddling sales online.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You can have anonymous transactions, you can have parcels coming in from any part of the world; that creates a challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also face a challenge from new drugs, new psycho-active substances, where people take drugs and mix them with contaminants to lower the costs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another separate challenge is the new attitudes of our young people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is a certain perception, glamorised through media outside of this country, that drugs are cool and cannabis are non-addictive.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we are not careful, they can become our next generation of abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The mix − the students, professionals, people who are well-educated, good jobs and a new group of Singaporeans trying drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Parents may think it is not their children but, in the past three years, we have picked up 350 students, all levels from Primary school to tertiary and all backgrounds, as well as without a background of substance abuse in the family.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last year, for working professionals, more than 70 professionals, managers, including accountants and engineers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the drug abusers committed 12% of other crimes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Eighty-three percent of those in our prisons are in there either for substance abuse or they have a history of substance abuse even though the particular crime they committed was not related to drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you can see how much drugs can impact our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We call him Edy, a young boy, six years old, both parents were jailed for drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He happened to be in the care of another person called Johan.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Johan was also a drug abuser, forms an ecosystem, a separate subculture.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Johan slapped around Edy, stomped on him repeatedly, on the six-year-old boy, killed him and dumped his body by the Kallang River.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You know there are thousands of such cases, not in Singapore but around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She had a stepfather, Mohd Johari, abusing cannabis, cough syrups, brought her home as a shield to hide his own abuse, thought that having her there, bringing her with him will prevent detection.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She was crying, he could not take it, he dumped her in a pail and killed her.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those who think we should go soft on drugs, on punishment, what is your solution to the thousands of "Edys" and "Noinois" around the world who are neglected, abused and suffering?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at the trend, if I give a summary, you have a new generation of abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are younger, they have different profiles, backgrounds and the situation can again become more troublesome, even if it does not get out of control.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our primary duty must be to protect our society and our people and stand up together as a country.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Most Members' suggestions are in line with where we want to go.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I agree with Mr Christopher de Souza as well as the others who spoke.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will maintain a tough stance and we will step up.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will review our strategy for the new challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will differentiate between those who supply and cause harm versus those who are abusers and, where possible, we will employ a data-based, science-based approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our first line of defence has got to be education, preventive drug education.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have worked for decades with MOE − school talks, lesson plans, so that our young people will understand.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our people are going over to Iceland to look at how they send their messages across, because this is a generation that when you tell them "do not do this", they might go and do it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you need different approaches and Iceland does seem to have an approach that seems to work, but their problems are different, the scale is different.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we never believe that we have found the ultimate solutions for anything.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we have to work with parents because the parents are key influencers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The NCADA survey shows that if a parent interacts with the children, they talk to their children, the risks that the child will take drugs is much lower.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have produced a parents' toolkit for that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Young people are also heavily influenced by peer and environmental influence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we need to grow a pool of anti-drug advocates amongst their peers, amongst young people's peers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we need volunteers, we need more individuals, we need more organisations, civil societies, interest groups, businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, effective enforcement and tough laws are part of it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will have to increase partnerships with overseas counterparts and we will have to tackle the new online supply menace, as Mr Christopher de Souza and others have mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will partner ICA, we will partner courier companies, postal companies, and we will move quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last year, ICA detected a suspicious parcel and alerted CNB.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Without that, that one kilogramme would have flowed on to the streets and destroyed more lives.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan talked about the recent acquittals and how it will affect sentencing approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Keeping our laws effective for deterrence, enforcement is a top priority.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will relook at the comments made in those cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have started doing it and will ensure that investigations are conducted thoroughly and impartially.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: AGC will help us study the Grounds of Decisions on that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The NCADA survey that I referred to also shows a very strong support for our tough laws.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People want us to be tougher on those who harm society, those who bring drugs in, those who provide it to others, especially young people, and those who encourage others.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will have to study how we deal with the issue of new psycho-active substances, how we amend the Schedules and what we need to do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members spoke about the amendments in 2012 to the Mandatory Death Penalty Scheme, in the context of drugs and drug trafficking, and whether they have been helpful.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We gave the Courts more discretion, where the trafficker is certified to have helped CNB.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What role does the death penalty play in this?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is an important part in our comprehensive anti-drug regime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And as I have said, part of an overall approach, which will not work on its own but it is a part of an overall set of measures − good judicial process, rule of law, enforcement, tough laws, education, rehabilitation and also DRC and LT.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are in a difficult situation, being close to drug-producing countries and we have maintained the death penalty as deterrence against trafficking.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is a large number of people that you are going to destroy the lives of.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And you multiply that by the number of family members.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Malaysia, the registered drug abusers numbered 280,000, as reported by the New Straits Times.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Indonesia, there are 5.9 million drug abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What is the nature of the drug trade today?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The finance comes from one country, could be manufactured somewhere in some terrace house, somewhere nearby Singapore, and couriers are easily available because they want to make some money.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do you believe that the death penalty has deterrent value?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you knew and you are outside of Singapore, you are in Malaysia or Indonesia, and if you knew that the likelihood of being caught is pretty high and that if you are caught with that amount of drugs, that you are most likely to face a death penalty, does that or does not amount to a deterrence?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Why do you think the drug kingpins are not in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun wants me to prove; how do you want me to prove?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Go and ask them, "You will not come into Singapore because of the drug death penalty?" Just remember that trafficking is a cold calculated offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The person decides to take a risk with his life, when he comes to Singapore for the sake of money.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, do not tell me they are poor, impecunious and desperate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They do not mind impacting the lives of 180 people each time.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun suggested that we change some of our laws.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As we consider how we proceed, why not consider the countries which have adopted your approach?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us not argue this in a vacuum.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: See what is happening in countries which have poor enforcements or have legalised drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I entirely accept Mr Kok's good intentions and the honesty of the views he has put forward.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But frankly, they will lead to the loss of many more lives and they will lead to more tragedy and serious grief for thousands.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the early 1990s, we were arresting between 6,000 and 7,000 people per year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, we are arresting between 2,000 and 3,000 per year; over a 20-year period.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That means, our drug situation, that demand for it has gone down.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at what you have said, first, you said that a person charged for an offence of importation is automatically presumed guilty once the prosecution shows that the accused was merely in possession of the package containing the drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because that, as a statement of law, makes no sense.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not know whether you wrote the speech, but that is simply not correct.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You have also suggested: there is a rule that involuntary statements are inadmissible but we do not really know what happens in the interrogation room; how statements are obtained on witness' testimony; and there is no requirement of recording of any kind.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In a drug case, Mr Kok, what needs to be proven?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What the drug is is a matter of scientific evidence; quantity is a matter of scientific evidence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, what are you suggesting would happen in witness' rooms that might lead to these suggestions that you have implied in your speech?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not know if you know how it works, but the prosecution will have to prove those things.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The defence will have to prove that the person did not know what it was, which is usually a defence that is run by many people, and you complained about that as well in your speech, because you say the onus must be on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt all the ingredients of the offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The usual variety of defences and let me read out to you a couple.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He said he travelled to Kuala Lumpur to look for job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was introduced to a man known as "Uncle". "Uncle" then passed him 10 packets of substances and taped these on to his body.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This chap then claimed he asked "Uncle" what they were for, but "Uncle" showed him three fingers in reply.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was not aware of the contents, and he came here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, you want the prosecution to rebut this?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is why our first Prime Minister, who was a lawyer, knew what the problems would be and reversed the onus of proof.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You talked about an "Uncle" you met in Kuala Lumpur; you show to the judge that there is such an "Uncle" and the "Uncle" told you all these things; and what was in your mind?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, again, I do not know whether you drafted this part of the speech or some lawyer drafted it for you, but you got to look at it in context.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was asked by one "Maren" to deliver items in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was told that it was rare and expensive, that it was wrapped up so that it could not be spoilt by coming into contact with air.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And so he went to Johor, met "Maren" and brought it over.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
