text: Or do you think it is fair that the accused should prove it?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have a favourite term for defences of this nature.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I call them as someone saying it is a shampoo for my pet toad that I got and I brought it into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if that is what you want to say, go and prove it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we are also dealing with thousands of Singaporean lives.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the person must get a fair trial.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Prosecution must prove what was the substance, how much was it, and possession, and any other evidence they can find.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the person has a defence, it is only fair that he proves it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So far, all these points, while I may disagree with the Member, I can see where he is coming from.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the next point he makes, and let me quote him, he said he would like to "speak on the humanity of the families of those executed and those who have their loved ones on death row.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: While we do not see it, the reality is that our criminal punishment, the death penalty, creates a new class of victims in the families of the death row inmates.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They found themselves having their loved ones taken away from them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In conversation with a former death row convict who was acquitted by our Court of Appeal, I am struck by the poignancy of how he described the impact of the death penalty on his family." But should not our hearts also go out to the victims, the "Edys" and the "Noinois", the girl who was four months old that Mr Christopher de Souza described, who was in the car locked up while her mother was dazed by drugs?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, you spoke with someone who was in this situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have spoken with many of the victims and their families − a lot of them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Prof Michael Hor that Mr Kok Heng Leun quoted was my classmate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And he knows and he has said – in the same conference that Mr Kok referred to – he knows this Government and he does not see that it will change its position on drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The question then is: do you want to take the risk of dismantling one key part of the deterrence that we have and take a chance?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You also say in one part, Mr Kok: is the approach really to put in tougher laws?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But at the same time, you also say you accept that the current enforcement is good and the current legal framework is good, other than the death penalty.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think you should, when you make a statement like that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I told you the backgrounds vary, their education backgrounds vary.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if you go and look at the backgrounds in other countries, you will see a whole strata of people getting into drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Shanmugam, you are close to your time limit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, if I put together the points that Mr Kok has made: first, it is the fault of the socio-economic gaps; second, we should make our laws less strict; third, we should do away with the death penalty; and, fourth, we should give a lot of empathy to the drug abusers and their families.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Pray tell me where that will lead us and how that will solve the drug issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You think the drug kingpins who want to make millions out of bringing drugs into Singapore will then be deterred?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The couriers who want to make money by bringing it into Singapore, they will be deterred because we show them a lot of empathy?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the abusers in Singapore will be transformed as well?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You just have to look at the example of other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In all of these, in public policymaking, you need a soft heart; you need compassion and that is what defines a civilised human being.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you can never have a soft head.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the heart alone rules policy, you are done for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will say this: as a parliamentarian, you have a right to make these points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as Minister for Home Affairs, I do not have the right to give effect to any suggestion which I believe will harm thousands of people and ruin our society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, it is my duty to do the reverse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Support for our penalties amongst our population, as Members know, is very high.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: NUS conducted a survey on public opinion in 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the NUS survey also presented a nuanced picture of public support for the death penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The support dropped when this question was asked, that if it can be shown that the death penalty was no more effective as a deterrent to others like life imprisonment, or a very long prison sentence, that means it is not effective and you can substitute it with something else; if you ask people that question, yes, the support then drops.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it is suggested that innocent people could have been executed, then the support drops.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a certain framework is put into the question and then you get a number and you come to the Government and say, "Therefore, change your policy", we have to look at the questions you asked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in any event, this is one of those areas where the Government has the duty to assess the facts carefully, the data carefully, and come to the best judgement that it can.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said in public, no Government glorifies in having the death penalty or imposing it on anyone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they do it, they do it with a heavy heart.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you do it because of the greater public good.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you do it based on your best judgement and assessment, not on the basis of advice given by people who argue from an ideological point of view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will listen to anyone with a good point of view, and we will make up our mind.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Abusers, as Mr Christopher de Souza and others have said, must be committed to kicking the habit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Nominated Member of Parliament Kuik Shiao-Yin said, can we consider shortening the incarceration period because of the impact it has on the families?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The incarceration periods are looked at regularly, whether it is for DRC, or whether it is for LT1, LT2.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a set of reasons why we have structured it as DRC and then LT1 and LT2.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is some methodology behind it and we continuously review the methodology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in the end, it has to, first, serve as a deterrence; second, keep society from being harmed by that individual; and third, what is necessary for that individual to rehabilitate him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The environment that is chosen will depend on what the individual needs, and I will explain that in a while.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every abuser has different risk levels and different motivational factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other programmes include family programmes, skills training and religious services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For lower risk inmates, they have a day release programme, they go for work or study during the day, minimises disruption.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are placed on community-based programmes to reconnect to the community, to help them transition to normal life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some are at halfway houses, some go home and community support is instrumental, we recognise that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some Members mentioned rehabilitation for young people, including Asst Prof Mohan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, we look at the young people, if they are lower risk, then they go for what we call the youth enhanced supervision scheme which involves counselling and case work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Others go to the Community Rehabilitation Centre (CRC) which I have just talked about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we will also look at some of the suggestions that Members have mentioned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Rehabilitation is something the Singapore Prison Service is very passionate about, as can be seen from the Yellow Ribbon programme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We think we should try to pick them up even before they commit an offence based on some profiles and we should try to change behaviour before.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we fail in that and they come in, we should try to change behaviour inside.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when they go out, we should also try to support them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And anything that works, based on science, based on evidence, we will be prepared to consider.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I accept it is crucial to help abusers stay strong when they come out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are structured family programmes in prisons, skills to strengthen the bonds, joint sessions with the family.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not saying by any means that it is perfect and that it cannot be improved or that we are where we want to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we have thought about these things, we have introduced these and they continue to be refined, changed, worked on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Singapore Prison Service has set up a Family Resource Centre, it has got the Yellow Ribbon community project to encourage families to visit abusers in DRCs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Family relationships are complex, different families, different types of relationships.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have volunteers who continue to follow up via the Yellow Ribbon Community Project.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have talked to the Association of Muslim Professionals who have said they will come in to provide family casework in their new rehabilitation programme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Salim started abusing substances in his teens, 20 years, two decades.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At one point, he lost his family support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was moved and struck by the unwavering support from the staff of Pertapis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has now been clean for more than 10 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is paying it forward as Chairman of the family support group for Pertapis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He strongly believes in not giving up on abusers even when their families have given up on them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He himself has experienced how community support can change lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Asst Prof Madhev Mohan said rehabilitation is important.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may be that, in Singapore, our message on deterrence and our tough laws have been so strong that the fact that we put a lot of emphasis on rehabilitation probably has not come through.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you can take it that we put a lot of effort on rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also referred to a specific case where he felt the prosecutors made submissions which were perhaps not appropriate or a bit too harsh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member knows that I do not control prosecutors' submissions; nor should I, nor would you want me to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I will certainly pass on what you said to the AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For young drug abusers, the emphasis has to be on rehabilitation, so that they can have a drug-free life ahead of them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Higher risk young people will require more intensive rehabilitation, they will be in the DRC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Often, we find that the parents are not willing to come forward.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have asked my people to consider whether, legislatively, we can do something, that the parents also have a duty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Coming back to some of the points that Members have made, on the international front, we do not want to be isolated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Within ASEAN, yes, members, in their domestic situation, may take different approaches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But they sign up to refusing to accept the legalisation of drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They continue to support criminalisation and there is an ASEAN coalition supporting it and there are a few other countries which adopt the same approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to have a sensible dialogue with others of a different persuasion and perhaps agree that they have their viewpoint and we have our own viewpoint.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Different countries should be allowed to have different viewpoints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we need the community's support and it must be a national priority to keep drugs under control.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today's Motion and the speeches of the Members, even Mr Kok Heng Leun's speech, give me considerable comfort because I think we are on the same page, that this has to be taken seriously and you reflect the perspectives in the world of the people in many ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given that there is a broad variety of viewpoints that have been expressed, almost everyone consistently supporting a strong stand, save for some difference on the part of Mr Kok relating to specific penalties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that shows where the weight of public opinion stands on this.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Please seek your clarification and not make another speech.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Yes, but I think some things I need a bit of time to articulate.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: My personal experience when I was young living in Geylang in the 1970s where the back alleys had so many gangsters and drug problems.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I have gone through the experience with my mom telling me not to go out by the back alley because it is dangerous.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, those experiences are real for me to say —

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Thirdly, I want to address also the issues about the social gaps which I mentioned in my speech.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In this particular case, a lot of them because of their experience and in that condition, that makes them very susceptible to take up addictions, like drug addictions or alcoholic addictions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, I am referring to that rather than a critique on the system.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I want to also reiterate that I have equal and not any lesser empathy for the families of the drug abusers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Again, my experience has told me − I have seen a lot of them − it is that philosophical stand, especially in terms of the death penalty, that I have problems with, personally.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: With regard to all the rebuttals that the Minister had in terms of the whole criminal investigation process, I take the Minister's point.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I will go back and do more homework.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I think that is very interesting, that is something that I am learning.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I will take that and go back and work on it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: When we have enough time, we can probably have another discussion.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister, would you like to respond to that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Vigilance, Mr Kok, is not a substitute for other things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need vigilance, we also need the other aspects that I spoke about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If so, what do you think we can do about it or what more do you think we can do about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People are entitled to have different viewpoints on that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What they have shared is insightful and appreciated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Dr Tan Wu Meng has expressed, "policy choices… set the tone for decades… and shape the lives of a generation." We have to stay vigilant for the sake of those who fall prey to harmful drugs and their families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is important that the laws send a strong signal to those thinking of trafficking that it is not worth the transaction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Minister Shanmugam has highlighted − this is a battle − it is regional and it is organised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That is the nature of what we are facing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Ms Tin Pei Ling has shared, stiff penalties are not something anyone would wish to see applied and yet they are necessary, necessary for deterrence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Alex Yam touched on the importance of our laws which deter the supply of drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While they may differ on how the laws should be carried out, there is something in common that binds − the need to ensure that our drug supply laws are relevant enough to stem the supply of drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To that end, I had suggested a regular review of the Misuse of Drugs Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Some contaminants increase potency and lower the cost to produce.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This does not just restrict but also deter the supply of such drugs before they can gain a sizeable demand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Technology transcends geographical boundaries and, in this instance, it has turned dark.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Through the Dark Net, drugs have become accessible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In a BBC documentary, a journalist ordered drugs online.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It was an eBay-like user experience, it was in quick order processing time of mere hours and there was a delivery in ordinary-looking packages containing the drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is a headline from the New Straits Times.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It reads: "Drug pushers using WhatsApp, WeChat to sell, recruit school kids".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This was dated just two months ago, 2 February 2017.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We must be wary that social media can turn into a Trojan horse if left unwatched.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Besides the Internet component, the other suggestion is the need to tackle the upward trend of drug abuse among those under 30.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This trend has been raised by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Dr Intan Mokhtar has highlighted through her stories, this is, indeed, a worrying trend.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Please look at the top of the graph.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is the situation we are dealing with.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To this end, the thrust of my third to sixth suggestions was to introduce new provisions in the Misuse of Drugs Act to deter trafficking and recruitment via the Internet, especially among those under 30 years of age.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our strong deterrent laws garnered support from Mr Vikram Nair, Ms Tin Pei Ling, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, Mr Alex Yam and Dr Tan Wu Meng.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They agreed that strong deterrent laws continue to be important and have played an important part in Singapore's relative success.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While they look at the need for deterrent laws to the drug abuser to stay away from drugs, they also recognised the need to rehabilitate, reintegrate and restore the drug abuser into society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin puts it quite nicely, we are holding "both punitive justice and restorative mercy in tension", "a strong anti-drug stance against the traffickers paired with an equally strong pro-rehabilitation stance for the addicts." An integral part and an important part is the family − this is because the family and the children suffer, too, when the drug abuser is put into incarceration for extended periods of time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Ms Kuik has put it, "The last thing we want is for kids to grow up motherless or fatherless which in turn increases the next generation's risk of falling into similar patterns of drug abuse and incarceration." Mr Louis Ng expressed the importance of reaching out to the family within the first week.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: An important initiative, as mentioned by Minister Shanmugam, is the Yellow Ribbon Community Project.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the second phase of the project, grassroots volunteers reach out to the new inmates' families by visiting them and grafting them into the community through events.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They also connect them with much-needed resources and practical support.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Accountability and effectiveness are enhanced through regular communication and updates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Louis Ng had also an interesting insight to share: "The drug consumption might be the symptom of a problem… The lack of strong family bonds might   the reason they consumed drugs in the first place." Supplementing the hon Member's point, I would like to share one example of a type of family therapy that addresses these problems.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There is a family therapy intervention exercise described in Friedman and Granick's book entitled Family Therapy for Adolescent Drug Abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It seeks to restructure the maladaptive aspects of the family system, such as, crisis management, guilt and the burden of redemption and, thereafter establish a method for controlling or eliminating substance abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It also includes education about the effects and dependence process of drug use.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Louis Ng and Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin have given moving examples of how bonding with children may be the best motivation for rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One, in particular, that stood out for me is inmate mothers recording bedtime stories for their children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This just shows how a small gesture can go a long way.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We should move beyond increased visitation time and increase such precious bonding opportunities to form a cornerstone of rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan has highlighted the need for rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Perhaps something that could be looked into, alongside what Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin raised on art-based rehabilitative programmes, is reconditioning, the over-writing of old thought patterns by new ones.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One example is Healing Broken Circles in Ohio, which does rehabilitation programmes in an incarceration setting. "Offered in a safe environment where participants feel they belong, learn concepts   master skills", its strength-based programmes provide participants healthy ways of expressing themselves, through art and courses of higher thinking and higher learning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These are important qualities to overcome the hurdles of reintegration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Again, we need not be so liberal in terms of the freedom provided, but it is nonetheless worth a study whether their programmes can fit into an incarceration model like DRC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin and Nominated Member of Parliament Mr Kok Heng Leun touched on the importance of accountability even through art − a key component, in my opinion, to good peer support and rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One example is Japan's Drug Addiction Rehabilitation Centre (DARC).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One of the reasons for the high rating from the users is "the companionship from recovered addicts and flexible frameworks to enhance drug addicts' motivation to recover." This is just one example of how positive peer support can be facilitated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The message to the former drug addict should be, "We want you to come back into the community".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Mr Alex Yam movingly shared, "the most important reassurance to recovering addicts is that they have a place at the table, that they are not abandoned by society." To have a place at the table, the former inmate must receive post-release support.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This looks to be widely accessible, yet personalised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: On the third point of the Motion, culture, there was broad support to resist pro-illicit-drug propaganda.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar, when we heard her talk about her son and what he faces in school, I was reminded again of how close to home this problem of drugs is.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It must not have been easy to share, but thank you for sharing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To add on to Dr Intan's point on the need to reach out to students and post-Secondary institutions, I think that it is important that students be taught the host of ills about drugs from a young age, but not just why they should stay away from drugs but also how to stay away from drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Dr Intan Mokhtar's account of her son has well illustrated, this battle is not far off.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Parents need to know that: (a) it is a matter that they should be concerned about and (b) that they matter − that parents matter.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Vikram Nair raised an important query whether the amendments in 2012 have caused a perception in the minds of potential drug traffickers that we have softened our stance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And if, indeed, MHA forms the view that the discretionary punishment mechanism has caused an increase in drug trafficking, we should seriously consider removing that discretionary mechanism and reverting back to the mandatory punishment regime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Given the consequences of drug trafficking to innocent victims in society, it is a legitimate query and needs to be responded to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Within this Motion, Nominated Member Mr Kok Heng Leun has questioned capital punishment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As mover of the Motion, I am prepared to tell Mr Kok what I believe in and why.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Nobody here cheers the idea of putting another person to death.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Nobody here wants to have to pronounce the death penalty on another person.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But I also care about the victims of drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We must also speak up for the innocent children of addicts who endure weeks, months, years of emotional neglect, physical neglect and abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I also care for the addicts who suffer slow and lingering deaths and the victims of violent drug-related crimes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Introducing people to drugs through drug trafficking results in slow and agonising deaths for them and years of pain for their families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In response to the Nominated Member, let me provide an explanation on practical grounds first.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Then, I will explain the principle and justifications following that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I do not disrespect the Nominated Member's view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is just that I do not agree with them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Any discussion on capital punishment must start with a query whether our legal system offers the environment needed to ensure that capital punishment does deter future drug trafficking crimes or, at least, reduces the incidence of such future crimes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But I believe our system does have the attributes required to ensure that punishments meted out by the Courts, including capital punishment, do deter future crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is because we are a society governed by the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Second, the investigative body in the form of the Singapore Police Force and the Central Narcotics Bureau is impartial and efficient.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is the merit of our system − an independent assessment of the facts by three independent judges.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That would make the process even more thorough for the sake of the trafficker.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And I hope the suggestion will be considered.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Third, within that rubric of rule of law, the potential offender, in this case, the potential drug trafficker, knows that if he is caught in Singapore, the law will be applied against him.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He cannot bribe or manoeuvre out of the reach of the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, if the case is proven against him, he will receive the relevant sentence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Fourthly, when punishments are meted out, they are publicised so the potential drug trafficker knows that if he commits a certain crime, he will be punished.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That awareness is important to deter future crime, or diminish the incidence of future crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Singapore legal system is possessed with all of these attributes and so it is a conducive environment for the sentencing rationale of deterrence to operate in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The drug trafficker weighs profit to himself compared to punishment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And because of the attributes of our legal system, he knows that he will receive the punishment if he is caught and the case is proven against him.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is not in every country in the world that you have all those positive attributes at play within a legal system and we must work hard to keep those positive attributes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, my practical conclusion is that capital punishment can and does deter future crime in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is a system that works well now and, until and unless a better and more effective system can be set up, I say we keep the present raft of muscular laws.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If we take it away, there is every chance that the deterrence against future crimes will be removed or diminished.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But as for Singapore, in my view, it deters.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I first had to analyse the issue of capital punishment as a judicial officer assisting the Court of Appeal and as a prosecutor in the Attorney-General's Chambers when I first started legal practice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We had to search our minds; we had to search our inner selves, to do what was right by society and the individual alleged offender.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the AG's Chambers, I remember prosecuting a capital case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Because he wanted to steal money from his landlord to fuel his drug addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In this case, drug trafficking supplied a man with drugs and he eventually killed, murdered to fuel his addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I knew that the consequences of a case proven will lead to capital punishment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is never easy but it is required.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As a judicial officer, I worked closely with the Court of Appeal, then-Chief Justice Yong Pung How and Judge of Appeal Chao Hick Tin.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Capital appeals would go up for hearing and I would support the judges by analysing the arguments on appeal with them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I remember one case clearly where the capital punishment decision was reversed and the offender was given 10 years' imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In each instance, all those individuals, all those involved, had to think deeply about what was right in each case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: From those experiences, I now know the importance of what we discuss and debate in this House when we make laws for our land.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I am convinced that we should not remove a needed legal weapon, in the form of capital punishment, in our fight against drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To remove it, in my view, would be to harm even more innocent victims.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Fifteen milligrammes of diamorphine sustain 180 abusers for a week.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Assuming four members per addict, that is 900 people affected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As regards my example of 900 people, for how long are they affected?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If the drug is highly addictive, that addict would be on it for years, psychologically killing himself and his family, slowly, over weeks, months, years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The real question we have to ask ourselves today is whether we, as a society, want to risk a potential increase in the supply of life-destroying drugs into Singapore, higher number of addicts, higher number of innocent families destroyed if we remove capital punishment for drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Protecting the hard, muscular position against drug trafficking protects even more innocent victims plunging into the horrendous clutches of addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I would also like to ask a few questions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What if drugs were offered to your children in the playground, any of our children in the playground?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What if drugs were offered to your or our children in school?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Once they consume them, there is every chance their health, their mental well-being, their futures will be destroyed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How many of us have actually seen a drug addict, met with a drug addict?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I have visited the DRC on more than one occasion and seen addicts desperately trying to overcome addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Compassion for the trafficker who trafficked to him − a 13-year-old?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He was nearly 20 years old when we spoke.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: You want to have compassion against a trafficker who trafficks to potentially 13-year-olds?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When I studied in England and when I took a train from King's Cross, St Pancras, I saw a drug addict on the sidewalk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Flesh was present where her fingernails should have been.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I saw her offering herself as a prostitute so she could fuel her drug addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It left a deep impression on me to see a life of promise so devastated by drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the constituency I serve, in Singapore, just on Friday night, I met a former drug addict.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He wants to stay off drugs and pass his urine test.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He showed me a photo of himself in his youth, full of promise and health.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He now looks a totally different picture − tired, worn.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Yes, compassion for society, compassion for innocent children of addicts, compassion for families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In closing, Sir, drug trafficking is a coldly calculated crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What we debate today is a key decision.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I trust and hope that the House will hold, protect and defend that line today.
